problems.title: Endless elastomer layer in finite shear: what τ/G measures
problems.setup: An elastomer isolation layer under a satellite payload adapter is h = 10 mm thick and so long in e₁ and e₃ that it is modelled as infinite in both directions. It is bonded between two rigid plates with normal e₂. The bottom plate is fixed and the top plate slides along e₁, giving x₁ = X₁ + γX₂, x₂ = X₂, x₃ = X₃. The rubber is incompressible neo-Hookean, σ = −pI + μB with B = FFᵀ and shear modulus G = μ = 0.6 MPa. The measured shear stress on the plates is τ = σ₁₂ = 0.9 MPa and the plates carry zero normal stress, σ₂₂ = 0.

parts.ask: Find the top plate displacement u.
sol: σ₁₂ = μγ exactly, so γ = τ/G = 0.9/0.6 = 1.5

parts.ask: What does τ/G = 1.5 represent physically here?
parts.a: The amount of shear γ = u/h: the tangent of the tilt of material lines that started normal to the plates (tan θ = 1.5, θ = 56.3°)
w: The tilt angle itself, θ = 1.5 rad = 86°
The Green shear strain E₁₂
The stretch of the 45° diagonal fibre
sol: The line X₁ = 0 maps to x₁ = γx₂, so tan θ = γ
At small strain tan θ ≈ θ, the familiar engineering shear strain τ/G
E₁₂ = γ/2 = 0.75 is a different measure

parts.ask: Find the largest principal stretch of the layer.
sol: tr C = 4.25, det C = 1, so λ² = 4 and 0.25
The most stretched reference fibre lies along (1, 2)/√5, at 63.4° to e₁

parts.ask: Find the normal stress σ₁₁ the layer must carry to stay in homogeneous shear.
sol: σ₂₂ = −p + μB₂₂ = −p + μ = 0 gives p = μ
Universal relation for any isotropic solid: σ₁₁ − σ₂₂ = γσ₁₂ = 1.5 · 0.9
It comes from the γ² term in B₁₁: a second-order effect of finite shear, even in γ
The infinite layer carries it internally; a finite block would need this traction on its end faces

parts.ask: Examiner twist: a stick of chalk is twisted until it breaks. Its surface is in small simple shear. How does the crack run?
parts.a: Along a 45° helix, normal to the maximum principal tension σ₁ = τ
w: Across a flat cross-section, the plane of maximum shear
Along a straight line parallel to the axis
Along a 63° helix, the principal direction found above
sol: Pure shear τ has principal stresses ±τ at 45° to the axis
As γ → 0 the principal directions of simple shear approach 45°
Chalk and glass are weak in tension, so a crack opens normal to σ₁ and spirals at 45°
A ductile shaft yields on the transverse plane of maximum shear instead

problems.x: For a neo-Hookean solid τ/G equals the amount of shear γ = tan θ, and finite shear also needs a normal stress difference σ₁₁ − σ₂₂ = γσ₁₂.

problems.title: Inflatable boom membrane: rotation plus stretch by the numbers
problems.setup: A patch of incompressible rubber membrane on an inflatable boom deforms homogeneously with x₁ = 0.9X₁ − 0.5X₂, x₂ = 1.3X₁ + 1.5X₂, and its thickness ratio is x₃/X₃ = 0.5. Angles are positive counterclockwise from e₁ about e₃.

parts.ask: Find the stretch of the material fibre that started along e₁.
Find the largest in-plane principal stretch.
sol: In-plane C = [[2.5, 1.5],[1.5, 2.5]]: equal diagonals, so principal axes at ±45°
Eigenvalues 2.5 ± 1.5 = 4 and 1

parts.ask: Find the rotation angle of R in F = RU.
sol: θ = atan2(0.6, 0.8) = 36.87° counterclockwise

parts.ask: The small strain tensor ε = ½(H + Hᵀ) with H = F − I is applied to the e₁ fibre. What does it report?
parts.a: ε₁₁ = −0.1, a 10% shortening, while the fibre actually has stretch λ = 1.58
w: ε₁₁ = 0.58, the true stretch minus 1
ε₁₁ = 0.75, equal to E₁₁
ε₁₁ = 1.5, equal to C₁₁ − 1
sol: The 37° rotation makes H large; ε mistakes rotation for strain, while E depends on U only

parts.ask: Twist: in the current configuration, at what angle from e₁ does the most stretched fibre point?
sol: The reference principal axis is 45° (eigenvector of U)
R carries it to the eigenvector of V = RURᵀ at 45° + 36.87° = 81.87°

problems.x: F = RU splits a deformation into a stretch U along material principal axes and a rigid rotation R, and the Green strain depends on U alone.

problems.title: Carbon truss strut: transversely isotropic and weak in compression
problems.setup: A pultruded unidirectional carbon/epoxy rod for a space telescope truss has its fibres along axis 1; the 2-3 plane is isotropic. Properties: E₁ = 135 GPa, E₂ = E₃ = 9 GPa, ν₁₂ = ν₁₃ = 0.3, ν₂₃ = 0.45, G₁₂ = G₁₃ = 5 GPa. Tensile strength along the fibres is 2200 MPa. For compression use the kinking estimate σ_c = τ_y/(γ_y + φ) with matrix shear yield τ_y = 60 MPa, γ_y = τ_y/G₁₂ and fibre misalignment φ (rad).

parts.ask: Find the transverse shear modulus G₂₃.
sol: Transverse isotropy: 5 independent constants, E₁, E₂, ν₁₂, ν₂₃, G₁₂
The 2-3 plane is isotropic, so G₂₃ = E₂/(2(1 + ν₂₃))

parts.ask: In a bonded end fitting the rod carries σ₁ = 900 MPa with a clamping pressure σ₂ = σ₃ = −30 MPa. Find ε₂ in microstrain.
sol: ε₂ = −(ν₁₂/E₁)σ₁ + σ₂/E₂ − (ν₂₃/E₂)σ₃ (compliance S₁₂ = −ν₁₂/E₁, S₂₃ = −ν₂₃/E₂)

parts.ask: Find the compressive strength for a misalignment φ = 2.5°.
sol: σ_c = 60/(0.012 + 0.04363) = 1078 MPa, about half the tensile strength
Limit check: φ → 0 gives σ_c → G₁₂ = 5 GPa (the Rosen shear mode)

parts.ask: Why is the rod so much weaker in compression than in tension?
parts.a: Each fibre acts as a slender column held sideways only by the soft matrix; slightly misaligned fibres rotate, the matrix yields in shear and a kink band forms (microbuckling)
w: The carbon fibres themselves crush at a lower stress than they break in tension
Epoxy has a lower compressive yield stress, and the matrix carries the axial load
Poisson expansion splits the rod along its fibres, which governs both directions equally
sol: Tension is fibre dominated: the fibres carry the load straight
Compression is matrix-shear dominated through fibre rotation
Strength depends on τ_y, G₁₂ and φ, so manufacturing alignment matters

parts.ask: Twist: a better pultrusion process cuts the misalignment to φ = 1°. Find the new compressive strength.
sol: A 1.5° improvement nearly doubles the strength: kinking is very sensitive to φ

problems.x: A unidirectional carbon ply fails in compression by fibre kinking, with strength σ_c = τ_y/(γ_y + φ) that rises steeply as fibre alignment improves.

problems.title: Window sensor port in a pressurised fuselage: Kirsch by Airy
problems.setup: A small circular sensor port of radius a = 10 mm is cut in the skin of a pressurised fuselage far from frames and stringers. Remote skin stresses are axial σ_x = 40 MPa and hoop σ_y = 80 MPa (plane stress, plate large compared with a). Polar coordinates r, θ are centred on the hole with θ measured from the axial x direction. For remote uniaxial tension S along x the Airy function φ = (S/4)[r² − 2a² ln r − (r² − 2a² + a⁴/r²)cos 2θ] gives σ_θθ = (S/2)(1 + a²/r²) − (S/2)(1 + 3a⁴/r⁴)cos 2θ.

parts.ask: Which boundary conditions fix the constants in φ?
parts.a: σ_rr = σ_rθ = 0 on r = a, and the uniform remote stress as r → ∞
w: u_r = u_θ = 0 on r = a, and zero stress as r → ∞
σ_θθ = 0 on r = a, and the remote stress as r → ∞
σ_rr = σ_rθ = 0 on r = a, and zero displacement as r → ∞
sol: φ is biharmonic, so the stresses already satisfy equilibrium and compatibility
The hole edge is traction free: σ_rr and σ_rθ vanish there
σ_θθ on the edge is the unknown we solve for

parts.ask: Find the largest hoop stress on the hole edge under the remote biaxial stress.
sol: At r = a: uniaxial S along x gives S(1 − 2cos 2θ); along y it gives S(1 + 2cos 2θ)
Maximum at θ = 0 (on the axial line, edge tangent along the hoop direction): 200 MPa
K_t = 200/80 = 2.5 on the hoop stress

parts.ask: Find σ_θθ at r = 2a on the same line θ = 0.
sol: Total 98.75 MPa: within one radius the stress is nearly back to the remote 80 MPa

parts.ask: The port radius is doubled to 20 mm. What happens to the peak edge stress?
parts.a: It stays at 200 MPa: the stresses depend only on r/a, so a bigger hole spreads the same peak over a larger region
w: It doubles to 400 MPa because the edge stress scales with a
It halves to 100 MPa because the edge curvature halves
It rises by √2 because the stress scales with √a
sol: The Kirsch solution has no length scale besides a, appearing only as a/r
Hole size sets how far the disturbance reaches (a few radii)
Fatigue and fracture bring in absolute size; the elastic peak is size independent

parts.ask: Twist: cabin pressure plus fuselage torsion adds a remote shear τ_xy = 30 MPa. Find the new peak edge hoop stress.
sol: Remote principal stresses: 60 ± √(20² + 30²) = 96.06 and 23.94 MPa
Superpose Kirsch along the principal axes: peak = 3σ₁ − σ₂
3 · 96.06 − 23.94 = 264.2 MPa, at the edge points on the σ₂ axis

problems.x: At a traction-free circular hole the edge hoop stress is (σ₁ + σ₂) − 2(σ₁ − σ₂)cos 2θ, peaking at 3σ₁ − σ₂ for every hole size.

problems.title: Light gas gun barrel with a hot bore: thermal stress through the wall
problems.setup: The steel launch tube of a light gas gun for orbital debris impact tests has inner radius a = 50 mm and outer radius b = 100 mm. After a firing sequence the bore runs ΔT = 100 K hotter than the outer surface in steady conduction, with no pressure and free ends (zero net axial force). Steel: E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K. With K = EαΔT/(2(1 − ν)ln(b/a)), the hoop stress is σ_θθ = K[1 − ln(b/r) − (a²/(b² − a²))(1 + b²/r²)ln(b/a)].

parts.ask: What is the steady temperature distribution T(r) − T_b?
w: ΔT (b − r)/(b − a)
ΔT (b² − r²)/(b² − a²)
ΔT (a/r)²
sol: Steady conduction with no heat source: (1/r)d/dr(r dT/dr) = 0
T = A + B ln r
T(a) − T_b = ΔT and T(b) − T_b = 0 fix A and B

parts.ask: Find the hoop stress at the bore r = a.
sol: At r = a: σ_θθ = K[1 − 2b² ln(b/a)/(b² − a²)] = K[1 − 1.8484]
σ_θθ(a) = −209.8 MPa (compressive)

parts.ask: Find the hoop stress at the outer surface r = b.
sol: At r = b: σ_θθ = K[1 − 2a² ln(b/a)/(b² − a²)] = K[1 − 0.4621]
Check: σ_rr = 0 at both faces and ∫σ_θθ dr = 0 across the wall (no applied load)

parts.ask: Why is the bore compressive and the outside tensile?
parts.a: The hot inner material wants to expand more than the cooler outer material allows, so the outer layers squeeze it and are pulled in tension themselves
w: The bore is compressive because heat raises the elastic modulus there
Thermal stress follows the temperature itself, so the hotter bore is in tension
The free ends let the tube grow axially, which reverses the hoop stress
sol: Thermal stress comes from incompatible free expansion, αT varying with r
A uniform temperature rise in a free tube gives zero stress
Self-equilibrated: the hoop force across the wall sums to zero

parts.ask: Twist: the same tube carries liquid nitrogen, so the bore is 100 K colder than the outside. Find the bore hoop stress.
sol: ΔT changes sign, so every stress changes sign (linear elasticity)
σ_θθ(a) = +209.8 MPa (tensile at the bore)
A cold bore is in hoop tension, at the surface where cracks start in brittle or cryogenic steels

problems.x: A radial temperature gradient puts the hotter surface of a thick cylinder in hoop compression and the cooler surface in hoop tension, with σ_rr = 0 at both faces.

problems.title: Pilot balloon with a Mooney-Rivlin skin: peak, valley and snap
problems.setup: A rubber pilot balloon for wind tracking is a thin incompressible spherical membrane of unstretched radius R = 100 mm and thickness H = 0.25 mm. Its rubber follows Mooney-Rivlin, W = C₁(I₁ − 3) + C₂(I₂ − 3) with C₁ = 0.18 MPa and C₂ = 0.018 MPa. Under equibiaxial stretch λ = r/R, λ₃ = λ⁻² and energy balance P dV = 4πR²H dW gives P = (H/(Rλ²)) dW/dλ.

parts.ask: Find the inflation pressure at λ = 2.
sol: I₁ = 2λ² + λ⁻⁴, I₂ = λ⁴ + 2λ⁻²
dW/dλ = 4(λ − λ⁻⁵)(C₁ + C₂λ²)
P = (4H/R)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷)(C₁ + C₂λ²)

parts.ask: Find the stretch at the pressure peak.
sol: Maximise f(λ) = (λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷)(1 + 0.1λ²) with C₂/C₁ = 0.1
f′(λ) = 0 numerically: λ = 1.476, P_peak = 1.342 kPa
Neo-Hookean (C₂ = 0) peaks at 7^(1/6) = 1.383; C₂ delays the peak

parts.ask: Find the stretch at the pressure valley that follows the peak.
sol: Second root of f′(λ) = 0: λ = 3.143
P_valley = 1.137 kPa
Beyond it the pressure climbs again

parts.ask: Why does this balloon re-stiffen at large stretch?
parts.a: The C₂ term grows like λ⁴ in I₂, so the factor C₁ + C₂λ² eventually outruns the falling geometric factor λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷
w: The wall thickens at large stretch, so it carries more load
Incompressibility raises the hydrostatic pressure p inside the rubber
The C₁ term grows like λ⁴ and dominates at large stretch
sol: Thinning (λ⁻²) and growing radius (λ) make the geometric factor fall like 1/λ
Neo-Hookean: P ∝ λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷ keeps falling after the peak
Mooney-Rivlin: P ∝ C₂λ at large λ, a rising branch

parts.ask: Twist: the balloon is filled from a regulator that raises pressure slowly. When P passes the peak the balloon snaps. Find the stretch it jumps to.
sol: Under pressure control the state jumps to the rising branch at the same pressure
λ = 5.70: the radius leaps from 148 mm to 570 mm

problems.x: A Mooney-Rivlin balloon shows a pressure peak, a valley and then a rising branch, because the C₂ term grows with λ² and outruns the geometric softening.
